newsitem.title: USA: Mississippi court stays release of Liggett papers.
newsitem.headline: Mississippi court stays release of Liggett papers.

text.p: The Mississippi Supreme Court Friday stayed the release of internal documents from Brooke Group Ltd's Liggett Group until 6 p.m. EDT April 11.
In a brief two-page order signed by Chief Justice Dan Lee, the court said: "The limited stay is being granted so that this court may properly consider the issues raised."

The stay came two hours before a 5 p.m. EST deadline imposed by Jones County Circuit Court, after which 11 Liggett documents would have been released to plaintiffs in a $650 million second-hand smoke lawsuit against cigarette makers.

The documents were among the records that Liggett agreed to turn over last week in a settlement with 22 states, which are suing the tobacco industry to recoup an estimated $30 billion in Medicaid funds spent treating poor people for smoking-related illnesses.
Jones County Circuit Judge Billy Joe Landrum ruled Wednesday that the documents could be turned over to attorneys for the family of Burl Butler, a Mississippi barber who died of cancer in 1994.

The family contends that Butler, who was 60 and never smoked, died of the second-hand smoke he breathed in from the cigarettes, cigars and pipes of people who patronised his shop over the course of 30 years.
The suit alleges that cigarette makers knew of the dangers of smoking but concealed the information. Plaintiffs say the Liggett papers may contain information to back up that claim.
When Judge Landrum made his ruling, he also issued a stay so that tobacco industry lawyers would have until 4 p.m. CST (5 P.M. EST) Friday to secure a decision from the high court.
The appeal was submitted by two attorneys, including former Mississippi Supreme Court Justice Reuben Anderson.
"The circuit court's order threatens petitioners with immediate, irreversible harm by disclosure of information protected by the attorney-client privilege," the appeal said.
Judge Landrum concluded they were outside the scope of attorney-client privilege because they included statements by industry experts who were not meant to testify at trial.
